meta.titre: Circular Motion: Centripetal Force, Banked Tracks and Orbits

sections.contenu_markdown: On the bends of the Bamenda to Bafoussam road, a bus that takes a corner too fast either slides toward the edge or its passengers feel thrown against the door. Neither effect is a mysterious outward force: both come from the fact that going round a bend needs a force pointing inwards, and the road, the tyres or gravity must supply it. The GCE Advanced Level paper builds many questions on this one idea, from a car on a banked road to a satellite whose crew float freely, and the common trap is to invent a force that does not exist.

items: Newton's second law states that the resultant force on a body equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, $F=ma$.
Velocity is a vector, so a change in the direction of motion is a change in velocity.
An angle of $2\pi$ radians is one complete revolution, and the arc length of a circle is $s=r\theta$ when $\theta$ is in radians.
Newton's law of gravitation gives the force between masses $M$ and $m$ as $F=GMm/r^{2}$, with $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}}$.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Describing circular motion.** For a body moving through an angle $\theta$ (in radians) in a time $t$, the **angular velocity** is $\omega=\theta/t$ in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. One revolution takes the period $T$, so
$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f,\qquad v=r\omega$$
where $f$ is the frequency in revolutions per second.

**Centripetal acceleration.** Even at constant speed the direction of the velocity changes, so the body accelerates. The acceleration is directed towards the centre and has magnitude
$$a=\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\omega^{2}r$$
By Newton's second law the **resultant** force towards the centre must therefore be
$$F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=m\omega^{2}r$$
This is the **centripetal force**. It is not an extra force to be added to a free-body diagram: it is the resultant of the real forces acting, whichever of them point towards the centre. Because it is perpendicular to the velocity it does no work, so the speed stays constant.

| Situation | What supplies the centripetal force |
|---|---|
| stone whirled on a string | tension in the string |
| car on a flat bend | friction between tyres and road |
| car on a frictionless banked bend | horizontal component of the normal reaction |
| planet or satellite in orbit | gravitational attraction |
| electron in a magnetic field | magnetic force |

There is no "centrifugal force" acting on the body in an inertial frame. A body that leaves its circular path does so because the inward force is no longer enough, and it then moves in a straight line along the tangent.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a vehicle takes a bend on a road or track inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
With no friction, the only forces are the weight $mg$ and the normal reaction $N$, perpendicular to the surface. Vertically $N\cos\theta=mg$; horizontally, towards the centre, $N\sin\theta=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$. Dividing gives
$$\tan\theta=\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\quad\text{so}\quad v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$$
At this design speed no sideways friction is needed. At a higher speed friction must act down the slope as well; at a lower speed it acts up the slope.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a mass on a string or a rider on a loop moves in a vertical circle, so that speed and tension change round the path.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Weight now has a component along the radius, so the tension varies. At the lowest point $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$; at the highest point $T+mg=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$. The string stays taut only if $T\geq0$ at the top, which needs $v^{2}\geq gr$ there. Conservation of energy between bottom and top gives $v_{bottom}^{2}=v_{top}^{2}+4gr$, so the minimum speed at the bottom for a complete circle is $\sqrt{5gr}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a satellite or planet orbits under gravity, or when the sensation of weightlessness is explained.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Gravity is the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, independent of the satellite's mass, and with $T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$ we get $T^{2}=\dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GM}$. Here $r$ is measured from the **centre** of the planet. An astronaut feels weight only through the contact force from the floor or seat. In orbit the astronaut and the craft fall freely with the same acceleration, so the contact force is zero, and the astronaut feels weightless even though gravity still acts and provides the centripetal force.

sections.enonce_markdown: A car of mass $1200\ \mathrm{kg}$ takes a bend of radius $85\ \mathrm{m}$ on a track banked at $18^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Taking $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and assuming there is no friction between the tyres and the track, calculate (a) the speed at which the car can take the bend without any tendency to slide, and (b) the normal reaction of the track on the car.

etapes.action: Identify the forces on the car.
etapes.justification: With no friction, only two forces act: the weight downwards and the normal reaction perpendicular to the sloping track. The centripetal force is not a third force.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Weight $mg$ (vertically down) and normal reaction $N$ (at $18^{\circ}$ to the vertical, pointing up and towards the centre).

etapes.justification: The car does not accelerate vertically, so the vertical components balance.

etapes.action: Apply Newton's second law horizontally towards the centre.
etapes.justification: The horizontal component of $N$ is the whole resultant force, and it must equal the centripetal force.

etapes.action: Divide the two equations to eliminate $N$ and $m$.
etapes.justification: Dividing removes the unknown $N$ and the mass, so the design speed does not depend on the mass of the car.

etapes.action: Substitute the numbers to find the speed.
etapes.justification: Use $\theta=18^{\circ}$ in degree mode on the calculator.

etapes.action: Find the normal reaction from the vertical equation.
etapes.justification: The vertical equation contains $N$ and known quantities only.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The bend can be taken at $16.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with no sideways friction, and the track pushes on the car with $12370\ \mathrm{N}$. Check: the horizontal component $N\sin18^{\circ}=3821\ \mathrm{N}$ equals $mv^{2}/r$.

items.erreur_markdown: My free-body diagram shows the tension, the weight and a centripetal force.
items.pourquoi_faux: The centripetal force is the name for the resultant of the real forces pointing towards the centre. Adding it to the real forces counts the same force twice.
items.correction_markdown: Draw only real forces such as tension, weight, normal reaction and friction. Then state that their resultant towards the centre equals $mv^{2}/r$.

items.erreur_markdown: The car skids outwards because a centrifugal force pushes it away from the centre.
items.pourquoi_faux: No outward force acts on the car. It continues in a straight line along the tangent when friction cannot provide the required inward force.
items.correction_markdown: The required force $mv^{2}/r$ exceeds the maximum friction, so the car moves along the tangent, which is outwards compared with the curve of the road.

items.erreur_markdown: The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the resultant force is zero.
items.pourquoi_faux: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which is a vector. Its direction changes continuously in circular motion.
items.correction_markdown: The acceleration has constant magnitude $v^{2}/r$ and is directed towards the centre, so the resultant force is not zero.

items.erreur_markdown: A wheel turns at $120$ revolutions per minute, so $\omega=2\pi\times120=754\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The formula $\omega=2\pi f$ needs the frequency in revolutions per second, not per minute.

items.erreur_markdown: Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because there is no gravity at that height.
items.pourquoi_faux: At $400\ \mathrm{km}$ above the surface the gravitational field strength is still about $8.69\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$, roughly 88.7 percent of its value at the surface. Without gravity the craft would leave its orbit.
items.correction_markdown: The astronaut and the craft are both in free fall with the same acceleration, so there is no contact force between them. Weightlessness is the absence of that contact force.

items.enonce_markdown: A ball of mass $0.30\ \mathrm{kg}$ is whirled in a horizontal circle on a smooth table by a light string of length $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ at a steady $2.5$ revolutions per second. Calculate (a) its angular velocity, (b) its speed, (c) its centripetal acceleration and (d) the tension in the string.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\omega=2\pi f=2\pi\times2.5=15.7\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

(b) $v=r\omega=0.60\times15.7=9.42\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(c) $a=\omega^{2}r=(15.7)^{2}\times0.60=148\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, directed towards the centre.

(d) The tension supplies the centripetal force: $T=ma=0.30\times148=44.4\ \mathrm{N}$.

**$\omega=15.7\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$; $v=9.42\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; $a=148\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; $T=44.4\ \mathrm{N}$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A satellite orbits the Earth at a height of $6.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m}$ above the surface in a circular orbit. Take $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}}$, the mass of the Earth as $5.97\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and its radius as $6.37\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate (a) the radius of the orbit, (b) the orbital speed and show that it does not depend on the mass of the satellite, (c) the period in minutes, and (d) the gravitational field strength at the satellite.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Orbital radius: $r=R_E+h=6.37\times10^{6}+6.0\times10^{5}=6.97\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

(b) Gravity provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, so $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$. The mass $m$ cancels, so the speed does not depend on the mass of the satellite.

$GM=6.67\times10^{-11}\times5.97\times10^{24}=3.98\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-2}}$ and $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{3.98\times10^{14}}{6.97\times10^{6}}}=7560\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(c) $T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}=\dfrac{2\pi\times6.97\times10^{6}}{7560}=5790\ \mathrm{s}=96.6\ \mathrm{minutes}$.

(d) The gravitational field strength at the orbit is $\dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}=8.20\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$, which is also the satellite's centripetal acceleration $v^{2}/r$.

**$v=7560\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, independent of the satellite's mass; $T=96.6$ minutes; field strength $8.20\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A stone of mass $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ is tied to a light string of length $0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ and swung in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (a) Calculate the tension at the lowest point. (b) Find the minimum speed at the lowest point for which the string remains taut all the way round. (c) State, with calculation, whether the stone completes the circle with the string taut.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At the lowest point the net upward force provides the centripetal force: $T-mg=\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, so $T=0.40\left(9.8+\dfrac{6.0^{2}}{0.90}\right)=0.40\times(9.8+40.0)=19.9\ \mathrm{N}$.

(b) At the top the string is just taut when $T=0$ and $mg=\dfrac{mv_t^{2}}{r}$, so $v_t^{2}=gr$. Energy conservation gives $v_b^{2}=v_t^{2}+4gr=5gr$, so $v_b=\sqrt{5\times9.8\times0.90}=6.64\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(c) The stone has $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is less than 6.64, so it does not complete the circle with the string taut. If it reached the top, energy conservation would give $v_t^{2}=6.0^{2}-4\times9.8\times0.90=0.72\ \mathrm{m^{2}\,s^{-2}}$. The tension there would be $T=m\left(\dfrac{v_t^{2}}{r}-g\right)=0.40\times(0.80-9.8)=-3.60\ \mathrm{N}$. A string cannot push, so the string goes slack before the stone reaches the top.

**$T_{bottom}=19.9\ \mathrm{N}$; minimum speed at the bottom $6.64\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the stone does not complete the circle with the string taut.**

items_markdown: Angular velocity $\omega=2\pi/T=2\pi f$ and speed $v=r\omega$; the angle must be in radians.
A body in uniform circular motion accelerates towards the centre with $a=v^{2}/r=\omega^{2}r$, so the resultant force is $mv^{2}/r$.
The centripetal force is the resultant of real forces (tension, friction, normal reaction, gravity); never draw it as an extra force and never invent a centrifugal force.
On a frictionless banked track $\tan\theta=v^{2}/(rg)$; in a vertical circle the tension changes round the path and a complete circle with a taut string needs $v_{bottom}\geq\sqrt{5gr}$.
For a satellite $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T^{2}=4\pi^{2}r^{3}/(GM)$; astronauts feel weightless because they and the craft are in free fall and no contact force acts, not because gravity is absent.
